bib.title: Multi-Turn On-Policy Distillation with Prefix Replay

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Multi-Turn On-Policy Distillation with Prefix Replay" (ReOPD). Baohao Liao, Hanze Dong, Christof Monz, Xinxing Xu, Li Dong, Furu Wei (Microsoft Research, Univ. of Amsterdam). arXiv:2607.04763v3 [cs.LG], 26 Jul 2026. Preprint. Code: baohaoliao/ReOPD.

COVERAGE: All 25 pages, 88,196 of 88,196 chars, including the abstract, theory, Tables 1-8, the analysis section, the conclusion and limitations, and the references (skimmed for origins). There are no appendices with results. The extraction is clean text. The figure plots are not extracted, so only the printed data labels are available. I did not read figure images.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: On math with a Python tool, ReOPD beats fully online OPD on the 4B-student average for every Qwen3-4B-student teacher setting. The gain is largest when the teacher-student gap is wide.
  number: 55.1 to 57.2 (4B teacher), 51.0 to 53.7 (8B teacher), 51.1 to 52.5 (30B-A3B teacher); the 8B student under the 30B teacher goes 56.5 to 56.8.
  setup: Qwen3 models. Teachers are Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, Qwen3-8B and Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507. The student is Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 (also Qwen3-8B under the 30B teacher). Prompts are 6.4K from DAPO. Macro average over 6 benchmarks. 200 steps, kappa=0.6, single run, no seeds or variance reported.
  quote: "With a Qwen3-4B teacher and Qwen3-4B student, ReOPD improves the average from 55.1 to 57.2; with a Qwen3-8B teacher, it improves from 51.0 to 53.7; and with a Qwen3-30B-A3B teacher, it improves the Qwen3-4B student from 51.1 to 52.5."
  where: p.15-16, Table 4
- claim: On search/QA, where the teacher stays reliable, ReOPD only matches OPD, with no gain.
  number: 40.6 (OPD) vs 40.5 (ReOPD) with the 4B teacher; 39.1 vs 39.0 with the 8B teacher.
  setup: Search-R1-style environment. Prompts are NQ+HotpotQA, 6.5K. Retriever is E5 over the 2018 Wikipedia dump, top-3. 7 QA benchmarks, 51,713 examples. Micro average. Student is Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507.
  quote: "With a Qwen3-4B teacher, OPD and ReOPD obtain 40.6 and 40.5 average accuracy, respectively; with a Qwen3-8B teacher, they obtain 39.1 and 39.0."
  where: p.16, Table 5
- claim: ReOPD is much cheaper to train. It makes zero tool calls during student training and is at least 4x faster per rollout.
  number: rollout seconds per step, OPD to ReOPD: 169 to 40 (math, 4.2x) and 64 to 7 (search, 9.1x). Including the teacher-resampling time: 79 (2.1x) and 14 (4.6x). OPD needs 32 processes for math and 80GB GPU memory for the retriever in search. Training takes under 3 hours on 8xH100.
  setup: Qwen3-4B-Instruct student, Qwen3-8B teacher (Fig. 1). Slime framework. The 169/64 versus 40/7 reading is inferred from the Fig. 1 data labels and the stated 4.2X/9.1X ratios.
  quote: "ReOPD is at least 4×faster per rollout than OPD." and "In Table 8, we take the time used for the teacher's resampling into account when comparing to OPD. Our ReOPD is still efficient,>2×."
  where: p.1, p.17, p.19; Figs 1, 6, 8
- claim: Core method. The prefix is replayed verbatim from a stored teacher trajectory, so the environment is never called. The student samples its own action at one step. The loss is per-token KL to the teacher along that student action. Positions are sampled with probability proportional to kappa^t, so early steps get more mass.
  number: kappa=0.6 default. kappa=1 is uniform and OPD-like. The weight is w_t = kappa^t, approximated from log br_t ≈ -(t-1)c̄, so kappa = exp(-gamma_t c̄).
  setup: the same kappa=0.6 is used across tasks with no per-task tuning.
  quote: "The student is on-policy only at the evaluated step, on top of a teacher-forced prefix." and "the step-decay surrogate setsw t =ω(t;κ) =κ t".
  where: p.9-12, Algorithm 1
- claim: Theory. The gap between the ideal interactive objective and the replayed objective is bounded by a student-occupancy mismatch term plus a teacher-reliability term. Fully student-on-policy is therefore not automatically optimal. The ideal mix between the two occupancies is a geometric bridge whose weight shifts toward the teacher with depth.
  number: Proposition 1, Eq. 4: bound = 2B·TV(d_student, rho_t) + E[eps_teacher-reliability]. The bridge is rho_t ∝ d_student^gamma · d_teacher^(1-gamma).
  setup: assumes the loss against the ideal target is bounded (B). The reliability error is not directly measured. Teacher support is used as a surrogate.
  quote: "Multi-turn OPD is therefore not just "make distillation on-policy" butreliability-aware prefix distribution design"
  where: p.3, p.7-8
- claim: Favoring early steps helps, and the gain comes from reliability-aware selection, not from using more data. A moderate decay beats uniform sampling.
  number: Fig 5b with the 8B teacher shows average accuracy of about 50.9 at kappa=1.0 up to about 53.4 at moderate kappa (values 53.4, 53.0, 53.4, 52.2, 50.9 for five kappa points; the order is read from the plot labels). Fig 5a shows that sampling mass on later chunks degrades accuracy.
  setup: student Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, teachers 4B and 8B. The label-to-kappa mapping is ambiguous in the extraction.
  quote: "the improvement from favoring early, low-shift steps shows that the gain comes from reliability-aware prefix selection rather than simply using more data."
  where: p.17, Fig 5
- claim: Prefixes from the teacher's own model work best. Prefixes from larger or stronger generators hurt, so reliability matters rather than raw capability.
  number: Teacher 8B, student 4B average accuracy. Prefixes from the 4B model: 49.3. From the 8B teacher's own model: 53.7. Plain OPD: 51.0. The 32B-prefix average is not clearly legible in the extraction (about 52.9 or 53.7 appears nearby), so confirm it from the figure before citing.
  setup: distillation target fixed to the teacher; only the prefix generator varies.
  quote: "prefixes drawn from theteacher's own modelare best, and substituting a larger or stronger prefix generator degrades the distilled student."
  where: p.18, Fig 7
- claim: The free by-product of teacher RL rollouts is as good as a dedicated stationary pool from the converged teacher.
  number: 53.7 (RL rollouts, mixed) vs 53.4 (final-teacher, stationary).
  setup: teacher Qwen3-8B, student Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507, math.
  quote: "Distilling against the final teacher from each pool gives nearly identical students, so the free RL by-product is as good as a dedicated collection."
  where: p.19, Table 7
- claim: In the multi-environment setting, one student trained jointly on math and search stays on par with OPD in both domains. Each environment's teacher trajectories can be collected separately and merged into one offline pool.
  number: math avg 55.4 (OPD) vs 55.3 (ReOPD); search avg 41.0 vs 41.0; the Cold Start student reaches 47.0 and 32.7.
  setup: single Qwen3-4B student, two domain-specific Qwen3-4B GRPO teachers. Teacher references: math 55.5, search 40.4. Data from both environments is concatenated and shuffled.
  quote: "ReOPD remains on par with OPD in both domains while avoiding online environment interaction during student training."
  where: p.16-17, Table 6
- claim: Off-policy SFT on teacher trajectories is clearly weaker than OPD or ReOPD on math.
  number: SFT 46.1 vs OPD 55.1 vs ReOPD 57.2 (4B teacher). SFT 45.0 vs OPD 51.0 vs ReOPD 53.7 (8B teacher).
  setup: same as Table 4. The Cold Start student scores 45.0. SFT and Cold Start are within about 1 point of each other.
  quote: "SFT 21.7 21.3 63.1 39.8 49.9 80.9 46.1"
  where: p.14, Table 4
- claim: Dense OPD supervision versus sparse RL (framing, taken from Thinking Machines Lab 2025).
  number: none
  quote: "RL supervision is sparse: a scalar reward conveys only a few bits per episode, regardless of how many tokens were generated"
  where: p.2

Smaller points. The 4B student under the 4B teacher (same model) reaches 57.2, above the 55.5 GRPO teacher. A note should be careful here, because the claim is about averages from single runs. In math, OPD wins some columns (Minerva 43.3 vs 42.9; Table 4). In Table 5, ReOPD is below OPD on Bamboogle (37.6 vs 44.0) for the 4B teacher.

LIMITS
- The authors concede that the pool's coverage and quality bound what the student learns.
- The step-decay is coarse. It measures depth, not distance from the teacher's reliable support. A learned or data-dependent reliability estimate may do better.
- The bound uses teacher support as a surrogate for the unobserved reliability error. Tighter, directly estimable reliability measures are future work.
- Gap-adaptive schedules are listed as a natural extension. The authors say a steeper decay is prescribed as the gap grows, but only one fixed kappa=0.6 was run.
- Not shown: any model family other than Qwen3, any student above 8B, or an environment beyond Python math and Wikipedia search. Browser, code and API environments appear only in the Fig. 3 schematic. Long-horizon agents are not tested: tool-call caps are 16 (math) and 4 (search).
- There are no seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests, and gains of about 0.1-0.3 are called "on par" or "slightly improves". The RL teacher is a Qwen3 model that went through an SFT cold start plus GRPO, with only 200 steps.
- Teacher-gap scale: the "wide gap" explanation is inferred from teacher size and from the math-versus-search contrast. The gap c̄ is not reported per setting. The regime explanation is argued, not isolated experimentally apart from Fig 7.
- The student acts only at one step per replayed prefix, so it is not on-policy along the prefix. The authors state this tradeoff.
- Dated: the experiments use Qwen3 models and the "Thinking Machines Lab 2025" OPD blog as the baseline. Fig. 4 is described qualitatively only (log r_t falls from about -0.36 to -0.41 by the axis labels).

BUILDS ON
- On-policy distillation: Thinking Machines Lab (2025) blog; MiniLLM, Gu et al. (2024); GKD, Agarwal et al. (2024); DistiLLM, Ko et al. (2024, 2025); speculative KD, Xu et al. (2025a).
- Sequence-level KD: Hinton et al. (2015); Kim and Rush (2016).
- Covariate shift: DAgger, Ross et al. (2011); scheduled sampling, Bengio et al. (2015); Ranzato et al. (2016); Professor Forcing, Lamb et al. (2016).
- RL teacher: GRPO, Shao et al. (2024); PPO, Schulman et al. (2017); DAPO, Yu et al. (2025).
- Environments and recipes: ReTool, Feng et al. (2025); Search-R1, Jin et al. (2025).
- Closest parallel: Wang et al. (2026) "dual exposure bias" in reasoning distillation, and Xu et al. (2024) "stronger models are not stronger teachers".
- Framework: Slime (Zhu et al., 2025); Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025).

CODE (verbatim, p.12, Algorithm 1)
"3: assemble candidate positions {(x, h_t)} from pooled trajectories ▷ prefix h_t: teacher actions A<t, teacher observations O≤t
4: draw positions with p_t ∝ ω(t;κ) ▷ early, low-shift steps sampled more often
6: student generates its action A_t = (a1t,…,ant)∼π_θold(· | x, h_t) ▷ token contexts on-policy; no environment call
7: accumulate Σj DKL(πθ(· | x, h_t, a<jt) ∥ πT(· | x, h_t, a<jt)) ▷ per-token KL along the student's action"
Training settings (Table 1): OPD and ReOPD use batch 256, lr 1e-6, constant schedule, 200 steps, temperature 1.0. Max generation 8192 tokens (math) or 4196 (search). The teacher is first SFT cold-started (3 epochs, lr 5e-5) and then trained with GRPO (clip 0.2/0.28, 200 steps).

FIGURES
- Fig 1 (p.1): bars for SFT, OPD and ReOPD on accuracy, rollout seconds per step, and tool calls per trajectory. It gives the whole payoff in one picture.
- Fig 2 (p.2): OPD loop versus ReOPD (teacher-forced prefix, student acts at step t, environment off, weights decay with step). It is the clearest mechanism diagram.
- Fig 3 (p.3): merging teacher trajectories from several environments into one offline pool.
- Fig 4 (p.10): log of the cumulative student/teacher likelihood ratio versus normalized step. It justifies using step index as a proxy.
- Fig 5 (p.17): ablation on chunk-sampling and kappa.
- Fig 6 (p.16): resource use (32 processes, 80GB).
- Fig 7 (p.18): prefix-source ablation.
- Fig 8 (p.19): rollout time including teacher resampling.
Captions were taken from the extraction; I did not run the figure-caption script or look at the images.

PROBLEMS
- No embedded instructions were found in the PDF.
- Extraction faults: math symbols are garbled in places (subscripts run together). Table 4's bold marks are lost inline, so the printed bests are merged into numbers (for example "77.843.358.2" is 77.8, 43.3, 58.2). Figure data labels are unordered, so the Fig 5 and Fig 7 values are partly ambiguous (flagged above).
- The first extraction call exceeded the output limit and was truncated at 40,000 chars; I re-read all remaining ranges directly.
- The paper reports Tables 4-7 as printed; Table 8 is referenced in the text but I found no separate Table 8 in the extraction (the corresponding data is Fig. 8).
